Critical values for the two-sided Kolmogorov test, corresponding to the sample size, are
given in Table A-10; for our sample of 16 values and a significance level of 10%, the critical
value is 0.327. The test statistic, 0.2819, is less than the critical value, so we cannot conclude
that the sample values did not come from the hypothesized normal distribution.
Note that Excel does not possess a Kolmogorov test statistic.
Two important observations should be made about the Kolmogorov test. First, the distri-
bution of the test statistic D is not dependent on the nature of the underlying population
distribution. Second, while the chi-square test of goodness-of-fit requires grouping possible
values of a continuous distribution into classes, no such grouping is required here. Thus, it
can be argued that the Kolmogorov test is better suited to situations involving continuous
distributions.

38.1 i ntroduction
Our tests thus far have been parametric, depending on the characteristics of the underlying
distributions. We now consider the class of nonparametric tests, in which we need make few
if any assumptions about the underlying distributions. In general, such tests are more widely
applicable than parametric tests but less powerful. We will examine nonparametric substi-
tutes for several common parametric tests.
The conditions necessary for procedures such as the t-test or analysis of variance do not
always hold in practice. For such situations we have a selection of nonparametric tests that
do not require conditions on the underlying distributions.
38.2 t he m ann-w hitney t est
The Mann-Whitney test considers the null hypothesis that two independent samples come
from identical population distributions against the alternative that the underlying popula-
tions are different. The test is most sensitive to a difference in the locations of the two popu-
lations, so it is often thought of as a nonparametric substitute for the independent sample
t-test (its effectiveness is not affected by the nature of the underlying distributions), and it is
assumed that the underlying populations differ only in location.
To perform this test, we take two independent samples, then order all the sampled values
together as one large group, creating order statistics and assigning the rank 1 to the smallest,
2 to the next smallest, and so on. Identical values are given the mean rank of the positions
they would occupy were they slightly different. The test statistic is based on these ranks.

population means using independent samples. In this way, ANOVA was an extension of the
independent samples t-test for the equality of two population means. The Mann-Whitney
test is a nonparametric substitute for the t-test that compared the central tendencies of two
populations; we now extend that idea to three or more populations with the Kruskal-Wallis

39.1 i ntroduction
This chapter describes the random number generation algorithms for distributions com-
monly used in business applications. Distributions are listed in alphabetic order for easy
reference. For each distribution, the key characteristics are summarized, algorithms
for random number generation are presented, and examples of their application are
provided.
39.2 t he b ernoulli d istribution
The Bernoulli distribution is the simplest discrete distribution. A Bernoulli variate can take
only two values, which are usually denoted as failure and success, or x = 0 and x = 1. If p
denotes the probability of success, then 1 – p is the probability of failure. The experiments
to generate a Bernoulli variate are called Bernoulli trials.
The key characteristics of the Bernoulli distribution are summarized in Table 39.1.
Table 39.1 Bernoulli (p) distribution.
Parameters: p = probability of success x = 1; 0 ≤ p ≤ 1
Range: x = 0, 1 1 - p, if x = 0
pmf: f(x) = p, if x = 1 f(x) = 0, otherwise
Mean: p
Variance: p (1 - p)
All figures and tables in this chapter appear on the companion DVD.
The Bernoulli distribution is used to model the probability of an outcome having a desired
class or characteristic, such as:
n A stock is up or down
n A sale does or does not reach completion
n A bit in a computer message is affected by noise and the message arrives in error
The inverse transformation method can be used to generate Bernoulli variates. Generate a
uniform (0,1) value u. If u ≤ p, return 0; otherwise, return 1.

The number of successes x in a sequence of n Bernoulli trials has a binomial distribution.
The key characteristics of the binomial distribution are summarized in Table 39.2.

The binomial distribution is used to model the number of successes in a sequence of n inde-
pendent and identical Bernoulli trials, such as:
n The number of items in a batch that have a certain characteristic
n The number of sales that reach completion
n The number of bits in a computer message that are not affected by noise
The variance of the binomial distribution is always less than the mean. The Poisson distribu-
tion can be used in place of a binomial distribution if the variance is greater than the mean
or equal to the mean.
Binomial variates can be generated in the following ways:
Generate n uniform (0,1) numbers. The number of random numbers that are less than p is
b(n, p). This is the composition method.
Compute the cdf F(x) for x = 0, 1, 2, …, n and store in an array. For each binomial variate, gen-
erate uniform (0,1) value u and search the array to find x so that F(x) ≤ u ≤ F (x + 1); return x.
This is the inverse transformation method.

40.1 i ntroduction
The purpose of this chapter is to provide the reader with an overview of the research process
which includes its logical and philosophical aspects, relevant ethics, and use of existing back-
ground. Hopefully, after studying this chapter, the reader will be able to answer the question:
“Is my research project noteworthy?”
But what is research? How is research accomplished? How can a research project be evalu-
ated? How can the research conducted be communicated? How and where can the results
of the research be implemented and applied?
A good starting point to resolve these questions is to look at the role the background review,
which contains and extends the literature review, plays in the entire research process.
Too often graduate students, many who are attempting to complete a research project for the
first time, mechanically follow the traditional template that resembles:
1. Formulate a problem statement.
2. Perform a background review.
3. Develop a conceptual framework.
4. State the problem statement as a formal hypothesis.
5. Choose and/or implement a design and the procedures.
6. Obtain the results (analyze the data).
7. Interpret the results and make conclusions.
Sadly, students have a tendency to think and implement this template in a strictly sequential
manner. As a result of their action, the student believes that the background review’s primary
purpose is to:
1. Begin by preparing a detailed annotated bibliography for the proposed problem.
2. Validate the originality of the research.
Unfortunately, the student perceives that every preceding step must be completed before
working on the current step.
Formulating and finding answers to questions is the primary purpose of research. In this
quest, the researcher must determine which questions are pertinent and which answers will
extend knowledge in the research domain. These research efforts can be accomplished using
exploration, description, predicting, and being explanatory. Finally, applications can then
naturally follow.

chunks.heading: 40.2 Conceptual Framework
chunks.sectionTitle: Conceptual Framework
chunks.content:
40.2 Conceptual Framework
A researcher must prepare for research through a continuous background review to
enable their ideas to discover noteworthy concepts in the research domain. Reading,
searching, intercommunity communication, and filing activities enable identification of
specific concepts pertinent to the proposed area of concern. These activities enable the
formulation of key concepts for the purpose of communicating with key communities in
the research domain of the topic. Eventually, the researcher compiles sufficient back-
ground to try their hand at creating a problem statement. The researcher needs to for-
mulate the research problem at a level formally complete so that the findings from the
proposed study have validity, and are related to other significant studies on the associated
concepts.
This is the actual beginning point for the real background review. A continuous background
review must be undertaken to find further studies on key concepts and their interrelation-
ships. Additionally, organizational and sensitizing activity begins. Included in this continuous
process is an attempt to find theoretical writings which may help in organizing.
The steps just described are the process of building a conceptual or theoretical framework.
Researchers maintain a perpetual review program, as a result they are constantly prepared
to identify problems for future research. As an idea occurs that is fruitful for future research
they file it away for reference purposes. Throughout the research they must reveal what sets
of concepts they are utilizing, concepts that assist them in defining problems, in collecting
data, and in analyzing the results to problems. Pertinent questions to ask during the develop-
ment and maintenance of a personal conceptual framework include:
1. Is the framework truly supportive in my research?
2. Does the framework enable a higher degree of efficiency in identifying meaningful
research problems?
An excellent article on constructing and utilizing a conceptual framework is Exploring the
usefulness of a conceptual framework as a research tool: A researcher’s self reflections by
Robyn Smyth in Issues In Educational Research, Vol 14, 2004 found at http//ier.org.au/
iier14/smyth.html.
Basically the suggested approach by Smyth follows the flows found in the following
diagram:
Notice that the background review and the conceptual framework are the bus structure
for this research circuit. Many two way interactions exist for the researcher to find assis-
tance in the fundamental research. Communication via the bus, the background review and
conceptual framework, enable researchers to determine the relevancy of the particular prob-
lem under study. This quest for relevancy leads to dealing with the issues of reliability and
validity.

40.3 Reliability, v alidity, u tility, and u sage
The reliability of a concept should be clearly distinguished from its validity. Reliability deals
with how well a proposed evaluation of the concept measures the concept. For instance, will
the evaluation of the concept consistently measure the concept. On the other-hand, validity
measures how well the concept measures reflect what the concept actually is about.
